0.note: Alternate translation: [This is a song that David wrote]

1.note: The psalmist is not using the phrase **my God** to mean that he possesses or controls Yahweh, but rather to emphasize that Yahweh is the God the one he worships. See the introduction to Psalms for further discussion. Alternate translation: [the God whom I worship]

Here the psalmist is speaking of going to Yahweh for protection as taking refuge in him, as if Yahweh were something strong or safe he could hide inside of. Alternate translation: [I always go to you for protection]

2.note: The psalmist is saying that, just **like a lion** would, his enemy would both rip his body apart and tear it in pieces. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they violently kill me like a lion ripping apart its victim’s body] or [they violently put an end to my life]

3.note: In some languages, translating verses 3–5 might require a significant rearrangement to make the meaning clear. This section presents a hypothetical situation where the psalmist calls a potential curse onto himself. You might have to connect each hypothetical situation in verses 3–4 with a consequence in verse 5, or even put verse 5 before the hypotheticals. However, it is important to notice that both verses 3–4 and verse 5 build up to a greater level of tension, with the peak of this tension at the end of verse 5. As you translate, try to capture this growing sense of hypothetical sin and its consequences, doing so in a way that feels natural to the poetic style of your language.

3.q: אִם־עָשִׂ֣יתִי זֹ֑את אִֽם־יֶשׁ־עָ֥וֶל בְּ⁠כַפָּֽ⁠י׃ אִם־גָּ֭מַלְתִּי שֽׁוֹלְמִ֥⁠י רָ֑ע וָ⁠אֲחַלְּצָ֖⁠ה צוֹרְרִ֣⁠י רֵיקָֽם
3.note: The psalmist presents a conditional statement that sounds hypothetical, but he is sure that the condition he describes is not true. He is making the case that he is not guilty. When translating, use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true (similar to how it is done in the UST). Be careful, though: if you choose to translate it as a statement of the opposite, as seen in an alternate translation, you will need to also change the wording in verse 5 to reflect this negation, as shown at the end of the provided example. Alternate translation: [since I have not done this, and since there is no wrong on my hands, since I have not repaid evil to one who was at peace with me, or senselessly rescued my adversary, then do not]

The psalmist is not using the phrase **my God** to mean that he possesses or controls Yahweh, but rather to emphasize that Yahweh is the God he worships. See the introduction to Psalms for further discussion. Alternate translation: [the God whom I worship]

Here the psalmist is speaking of **wrong** as if it were something that could be held in someone’s hands. Your language may have a comparable expression that you could use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [if I have done something wrong with my hands] or [if I have treated someone wrongly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrong**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [if I have wronged someone]

4.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I have acted evilly to one who was at peace with me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to my friend] or [to my peaceful neighbor]

This could mean: (1) being an unfaithful friend by saving a person who is the author’s and his ally’s enemy. Alternate translation: [or saved my enemy for no reason] (2) attacking an enemy without immediate cause (in this case the verb translated rescue could be taken as plunder). Alternate translation: [or plundered my enemy without cause] (3) not only doing evil to friends but even doing good to enemies. In this case the phrase would be less logically connected to the previous one. Alternate translation: [and I even rescue one who is my enemy without reason]

5.note: Here, **my soul**, **my life**, and **my honor** represent the whole person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [me … me … me]

This refers to lying dead and unburied in disgrace. (This is the same word for dust as in Genesis 3:19.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and throw my dead body on a dirt pile]
This represents capturing him. Alternate translation: [capture me]

6.note: **Arise** represents doing something or taking action. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Do something] or [Take action]

Here, **In your nose** is an idiom meaning that **Yahweh** is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Because you are angry]

Here, **be lifted** represents overcoming or conquering people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [overcome]

The **rage of my adversaries** represents their attacks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [against the attacks of my adversaries] or [against my adversaries who attack me]

The psalmist is speaking to **Yahweh** as if he were asleep and needed to **wake up**. Here waking up represents starting to do something or take action. It does not imply that the psalmist thinks Yahweh is asleep. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take action] or [Start to do this]

This wording serves a dual function: it both justifies the demands made earlier in this verse and sets the stage for the expectations expressed in the following verses. When translating, consider how to maintain this two-fold connection in your language, ensuring that it aligns with the logical and emotional flow of the text.

7.note: Alternate translation: [And let an assembly of peoples surround you]
Yahweh ruling the **assembly of peoples** from heaven is spoken of as being **over it** and **on high**. Alternate translation: [rule over them from heaven] or [rule over them]

8.note: The word **adjudicate** is used to show that in the original two different words meaning judge are used. If you have two terms in your language, you can use two; if not, you can use the same term twice. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, judge the peoples! Judge me, Yahweh]
The implication is that Yahweh will find the psalmist innocent. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Judge me innocent]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **integrity**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [according to how I live rightly and according to how I live honestly]
This could be: (1) a title for Yahweh. Alternate translation: [O you, Above All] (2) a clause locating the author’s righteousness and integrity in himself. Alternate translation: [which is in me]

9.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the evil things of]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in 1:1.
See how you translated the phrase **the righteous** in 1:5.

The **hearts and kidneys** are internal organs that represent peoples’ thoughts and desires in the author’s culture. If these body parts do not have that meaning in your language, you could use an equivalent expression that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [thoughts and motives]
If it would be more natural in your language, you could move the last clause in this verse to the beginning as in the UST.

10.note: The word **shield** represents God’s protection. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God protects me]

Here the **heart** represents the thoughts and motives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those whose thoughts and motives are upright]

11.note: The psalmist assumes that his readers will understand that God is indignant with the wicked. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and a God who is angry with evil people every day]

Here, **on every day** represents a constant state. God is angry with the wicked all the time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all the time]

12.note: In verses 12 and 13, David speaks of God deciding to punish the wicked as if God were a warrior preparing to fight against them with weapons. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God will prepare to punish him like a warrior prepares to fight by sharpening his sword]
The first **he** in this verse refers to the wicked. After the word **repent** all the **he** and **his** refer to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.

13.note: This could mean: (1) for the wicked, that is, God has prepared to use these weapons against the wicked. Alternate translation: [and for the wicked] (2) for himself, that is, God has prepared the weapons for his own use. Alternate translation: [and for himself]

14.note: These three phrases mean basically the same thing. The second and third emphasize the meaning by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. However, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the later phrases are repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [he who is pregnant with wickedness, who also conceives trouble, who even births lies]

The psalmist speaks of the things that a wicked person does as if the person were **pregnant**, and **wickedness**, **trouble**, and **lies** are the baby. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Just as a woman conceives a child, carries it to term, and gives birth to it, so evil people think of wrong things to do, they do those wrong things, and then they lie about what they have done] or [the person ready to do wicked things. He makes plans for trouble and produces lies]
Here the subject switches from God back to the evil person. Alternate translation: [the wicked person is pregnant]

Here, **he** represents evil people in general. It may be strange in some languages to use a masculine pronoun when talking about someone being pregnant or giving birth, even in a figure of speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a more natural expression. Alternate translation: [the person pregnant with wickedness, who conceives trouble, who births lies]

16.q: יָשׁ֣וּב עֲמָל֣⁠וֹ בְ⁠רֹאשׁ֑⁠וֹ וְ⁠עַ֥ל קָ֝דְקֳד֗⁠וֹ חֲמָס֥⁠וֹ יֵרֵֽד
16.note: Here, **trouble** and **violence** are spoken of as if they hit a person’s head or fall down on it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression in your translation or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His own destructive plans destroy him, for his violence attacks him] or [When he plans to trouble others, others trouble him; when he attacks others, others attack him]

16.q: יָשׁ֣וּב עֲמָל֣⁠וֹ בְ⁠רֹאשׁ֑⁠וֹ וְ⁠עַ֥ל קָ֝דְקֳד֗⁠וֹ חֲמָס֥⁠וֹ יֵרֵֽד
16.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **trouble** and **violence**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [His troubling others returns on his head, and his violently attacking others comes down on the top of his head]

17.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **praise**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because he is righteous and sing a praise song to]

Here, **name** represents reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s reputation]
